Back in 2010, when Mr. Lewis’s book came out, it was as ubiquitous an accessory for business-class airline passengers as the “Twilight” novels were for adolescent girls. Part of the book’s appeal — a side effect of its author’s smart, breezy, plain-spoken style — was that it offered readers the illusion of retroactive prescience. You could read about the insanity of bundling subprime mortgages into highly rated investment products and think: Well, of course that was a recipe for disaster. Of course a drop in the housing market would bring the whole thing crashing down like a Jenga tower. It was obvious. We knew it all along.

In fact, almost none of us did. Certainly not the government officials and banking executives who remain at liberty and in positions of power to this day. Or if they did know, they didn’t care. The truth about what the banks and their enablers were doing was obvious only to a handful of people (one of whom, in the movie, is shown demonstrating the Jenga tower metaphor I just borrowed). Mr. McKay, with a comedy writer’s eye for archetypes, sorts them into an amusing array of strongly defined characters.
There is the antisocial numbers guy, Dr. Michael Burry (
Christian Bale
), a fund manager who sits in his office wearing a T-shirt and flip-flops, blasting death metal, beating on his desk with drumsticks and betting his client’s money on financial catastrophe. There is the righteously angry crusader, Mark Baum (
Steve Carell
), a disaffected Wall Streeter who sees a similar wager as the perfect expression of his contempt for the big banks (including the one he technically works for). And there are the young indie upstarts, Jamie Shipley (Finn Wittrock) and Charlie Geller (John Magaro), college buddies whose “garage band” fund was started with their own money and who want to show that they can play in the big leagues.
Linking these motley iconoclasts, and serving as our guide to the apocalypse unfolding around them, is Jared Vennett, a silky cynic played, with all the seductiveness that has made him a beloved Internet
meme
, by
Ryan Gosling
. From time to time Vennett will cast his baby blues toward the camera to tell us that something didn’t really happen in quite the way it’s being shown — or that, incredibly enough, it actually did. His slick, winking wit inoculates the movie against excessive earnestness and allows us to think that “The Big Short” is going to be one of those boisterous, amoral rich-guy movies, complete with geysers of Champagne and visits to strip clubs.
Which, to some extent, it is. Mr. McKay is not above using paid-for female nudity as a signifier of capitalist excess, nor acknowledging, more generally, the hedonistic aspects of greed. He is a naturally exuberant director, and his antic energy matches the rhythms of the story. The teams conspiring to short the market are impossible not to root for, and the work of the movie’s sprawling ensemble is never less than delightful. (This is the place to appreciate the contributions of Rafe Spall, Hamish Linklater and Jeremy Strong, who play Baum’s baffled minions; Adepero Oduye, who plays his liaison to the bank that houses his fund; and Marisa Tomei, who as Baum’s wife is like the only civilian in a combat picture.)
But when we root for Baum and Burry to be proven right, for Shipley and Geller to hit pay dirt and for Vennett to earn the right to be smug in perpetuity, we are also hoping for ruin to be visited on millions of ordinary people. Houses, nest eggs, jobs and lives will be lost.
Brad Pitt
, in a gravelly turn as Ben Rickert, Shipley and Geller’s paranoid guru, makes this point explicitly when he scolds his protégés for celebrating their good fortune. He says what needs to be said, but the achievement of “The Big Short” is that Mr. McKay doesn’t only underline the moral of the story in dialogue. The film’s final images, its abrupt shift in tone from exhilaration to exhaustion, its suddenly downbeat music (by Nicholas Britell) all combine to trigger a climactic wave of almost unbearable disgust.
Because, as we know — and as we can stand, from time to time, to be reminded — there is no happy ending to this story, no punishment for the crime. A movie is unlikely to change that, and “The Big Short,” in many ways a startlingly ambitious film, is modest about what it can do. It offers no solutions, and no comfort. The best it can do is put down a marker.
“The Big Short” is rated R (Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian). All that is solid melts into air; all that is holy is profaned. Running time: 2 hours 10 minutes.

GLASGOW —  “Scotland has gone mad,” wrote Chris Deerin, a Scottish columnist, trying to comprehend the surge of nationalism only seven months after an independence referendum was soundly defeated by 10 percentage points.
“It’s a strange thing, starting to think that your homeland may be a bit dim,”
he wrote in a column for CapX
, produced by a research institution of the center-right. “It’s even stranger when that homeland is Scotland, cradle of the Enlightenment, engine of the Empire.”
The judgment is harsh, but the sea change in Scotland is one of the great dramas of the British election on May 7, coupled with
the collapse of the Liberal Democrats
and the rise of the U.K. Independence Party. If some Liberal Democrats are heading toward Labour, Scottish Labour
voters are flooding to the Scottish National Party
, which looks likely to win most of Scotland’s 59 seats, putting new momentum behind the uncosted notion of independence.
Even Glasgow, heartland of the Scottish Labour Party, is turning to the more fervently left-wing S.N.P. According to  constituency polling, the head of the Scottish Labour Party, Jim Murphy, could lose his seat, along with the shadow foreign secretary, Douglas Alexander.
A wipeout in Scotland could cost the Labour leader Ed Miliband a place  in Downing Street or force him into a deal with the S.N.P. And as exciting as all this may be for the Scots, it raises new doubts about the future of
Britain
.
A Scotland so dominated by the S.N.P. would mean that Labour becomes just another English party, like the Conservatives. Since the S.N.P.’s prime goal is independence, other Britons question whether Scotland should continue to benefit disproportionately from the wealthier south.
England funnels money north that pays for free university tuition and prescription drugs for Scots — benefits not available to other Britons.
Because of a regional formula, Scotland spends 10 percent more per capita than the British average. According to projections from the Office for Budget Responsibility, Scotland’s net fiscal deficit will be 8.6 percent of gross domestic product, compared with 4 percent for Britain.
That doesn’t matter in a unified country, but it will if the S.N.P. acts too purely in Scotland’s interests or presses its Scottish rival but putative Westminster partner, Labour, too hard for new spending.
The S.N.P. leader, Nicola Sturgeon, has impressed the rest of Britain in televised debates. She demands an
end to austerity
but is vague on how to finance it or reduce the deficit. Nor does she address collapsing oil prices, which would put another big hole in an independent Scotland’s revenue. But as Scotland’s first minister, she’s not even running for a seat. Her predecessor, Alex Salmond, is, however, and they want to force any Labour government sharply left.
Such talk pleases the Conservatives, who argue that a Miliband government dependent on the S.N.P. means
“chaos”
and “economic irresponsibility.” Boris Johnson, a Conservative, compared Ms. Sturgeon and Mr. Miliband to a scorpion on the back of a frog.
Then the famous
“West Lothian question”
becomes more acute — why should Scottish members of Parliament vote on matters affecting England, while Westminster politicians have no vote on Scottish matters? Those decisions are made by Scotland’s increasingly powerful regional government, run by the S.N.P.
With England representing 85 percent of Britain’s population, the Tories have already raised the question of “English votes for English laws.” Taken to its logical conclusion, that would mean separate parliaments.
The journalist Martin Wolf wrote in The Financial Times that
the S.N.P. as a “permanent kingmaker”
risks “the stability of the union.”
For “a party interested mainly in having its cake and eating it” to hold the balance of power, he said, “does not seem to me a price worth paying for the union.”

David Zaring is assistant professor of legal studies at the Wharton School of the
University of Pennsylvania
.
The
Federal Reserve Board
has not had to worry much in the past about invasive legislation from Congress. The current highway bill, however, represents the culmination of a change in the political risk the agency faces.
The bill exemplifies a new trend of legislative hostility toward the agency, which has expressed itself in Republican-sponsored bills calling for audits of the central bank, efforts to limit the Fed’s discretion in setting monetary policy and even calls for its dissolution.
Those bills had never gone far. But now, the tax-averse legislature has chosen to pay for new highway funding through two raids on the Fed’s budget. If this bill becomes law, it will represent a new and troubling interference by Congress in the affairs of the central bank.
The first raid drains the central bank’s “rainy day fund,” money set aside from revenue earned from its trading operations – it trades government debt to set monetary policy — to deal with the possibility of market losses.
The second raid reduces the dividend that the Fed has paid to its member banks. Since 1913, that dividend has been set at 6 percent. Under the highway bill, the new, lower dividend would track the rate of return on the 10-year Treasury note, currently around 2.2 percent, with the difference being used for highway funding.
It is the dividend reduction that represents a particularly novel degree of interference with the Fed’s internal workings.
Taking $19 billion from the rainy day fund’s $29 billion stockpile certainly affects the Fed’s internal budgeting. But Congress has done this before. The Fed turns most of its trading profits over to the Treasury Department anyway. Moreover, it has never lost money on its open market operations, meaning that the $10 billion that would be left over should suffice as an emergency reserve.
Reducing the dividends of member banks, however, is different, even if it concerns a pretty anachronistic Fed practice. The dividend comes from shares that the banks are obligated to purchase when they become members of the Federal Reserve System.
But it also harks back to the days when the Fed was set up as a semiprivate institution, owned by its member banks, but created by Congress.
Nobody thinks that the Fed is a private bank anymore, or they shouldn’t – it hasn’t looked like one since the New Deal.
The Fed has been explicitly charged with the public function of managing the monetary supply. It is run by political appointees based in Washington, nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. The era of a decentralized Federal Reserve System run by regional boards nominated by member banks is long gone.
There is no reason to pay Fed member banks a 6 percent dividend solely because they have always received a 6 percent dividend. It is strange for a government agency to pay a dividend to the industry it regulates, and perhaps that persuaded some in Congress to cut the dividend. But cutting the dividend to pay for a highway bill puts America’s banks on the hook for a roads project that has nothing to do with them.

Fed officials have warned that the dividend cut could lead to unintended consequences, and I can imagine some banks rechartering as state banks, rather than leaving their money at the Fed to earn 2.2 percent. I can also see the banks preparing a plausible court case citing the Constitution’s takings clause.
After all, the member banks had investment-backed expectations about that dividend that had a century of pedigree. It is not clear why they have been singled out so that Congress could do something about transportation without raising the gas tax.
Banks do not usually do well with takings claims — it is a heavily regulated industry after all, meaning that you are expected to put up with administrative surprises — but this time might be different.
Even worse, it all amounts to a real threat to the Fed’s cherished independence. Congress has talked tough about reining in the Fed in the past. But using the central bank as a fund-raiser for unrelated fiscal priorities is the sort of thing that happens in banana republics. And plundering the dividend for pet projects is the kind of thing no chief executive would be able to get away with.
I even worry about the politics of all these “take back the Fed” initiatives. Legislators have criticized the Fed for being too cozy with the big banks, but they have been very receptive to the political donations that come from those banks. I doubt a Fed that was used by Congress as a regular piggy bank would end up being used for far-reaching legislative ends.
Those in Congress who have been campaigning against the Fed have certainly won a round with the highway bill. It will doubtless increase their agitation to mess even more with the workings of the central bank.

I remember it raining a little.I remember there was popcorn.I remember we were both wearing white.I remember it was our first date.
My husband and I met on a singles hiking weekend July 4, 1983. I went home to Boston and he came back to New York. He invited me to New York for a long weekend in August. The weekend started with last minutes stage tickets for "Cats" , TKTs to see " Nine" , TKTS to see " 42 Street", a walk in Central Park, and the Bronx Zoo. Who wouldn't fall in love? We went on to see Cats eight times, including our tenth anniversary with our three kids. It's been 32 summers of love and counting.
We met through mutual friends at a music festival in Pennsylvania.  I thought he was weird.  I still wanted to see him again.  He brought me to Governor's Island, took my hand, pulled me towards him, and kissed me.  We've been in love ever since.
Nothing special, just some food on the grass watching kids run around. I grew up coming to this park so it was fun remembering all of that. And in our busy lives it was special in and of itself to just be able to sit, eat, and talk for an hour with nothing else to do but enjoy each other's company.
I went out with this guy, three or four times. I'm an opera singer and travel often for my career.We are at one of my favorite restaurants after a few weeks between dates. I ask him to pass the bread. He looks at me and says, "You'll take what I give you." After I laugh, this fool says, "You are not thin or pretty enough to hold my interest." At the time I was a size 2 and 5'8"--- then my pasta came and with tremendous sadness I stormed out of the restaurant. I REALLY WANTED MY FOOD!
He was skeptical of this weird Chinatown gem but the bar's random music and cheap beer won him over. 5 hours later, we stumbled outdoors into the pouring summer storm where we had the most movie-moment-esque kiss I've ever had. It became our favorite bar.
We met in line for the bathroom at Crown Victoria and he ended up taking my number. When he texted me later (around 3am) I invited him over to party with my friends on our roof in Brooklyn.  We all stayed up all night watching the crescent moon set and the sun rise.
Meet a guy off okcupid at la esquina for tacos. tacos turned into drinking and dancing in williamsburg and that turned into 4 years of dating.
I have been dating my girlfriend for 1+ 1/2 years, 85% of that time has been spent apart as we are pursuing educations in different states. I took her on a date to Governor's island. We ate leftovers and laid in a hammock for hours. The view of the city was spectacular. When you're in a long distance relationship, the perfect date is just laying together.  I said bye to her later that evening. As her bus pulled away I teared up and dreampt of the next time I would see her.
It was our third date and one of the first hot evenings of the summer. My native Brooklyn date wanted to show me where he grew up. We walked across the busy bridge while he told me everything about his childhood. Occasionally we would stop and look back at the Manhattan skyline and as we came closer to Brooklyn he got bolder with his tough. At first it was just a hand in mine, then he pulled his arm around my waist. Finally, at the last part of the bridge he leaned in and kissed me.
Nobody noticed us pouring wine into Starbucks cups as we sat on a park bench in Washington Square Park one evening last summer. We talked for a couple hours without running out of things to say. It was my first opportunity to figure him out. It was the best because we were surrounded by the sites and sounds of the city but we were only focused on each other. Plus, breaking the open container law is not something I normally do (especially on a Tuesday) so it made it memorable!
After getting my AIM screenname off of my profile on "nyu.thefacebook.com," he finally convinced me to (begrudgingly) meet him in person (...in my dorm room). He (6'3") turned out to be taller than I am (6'1"), so I decided to give him a chance after all. That was 11 years ago. (We're married now.)
My then boyfriend desperately wanted to show me Fort Tryon & Inwood parks that he explored as a teen. We went on what was the hottest day of July & managed to get COMPLETELY lost in Inwood Park. I panicked for a while, but he stayed totally calm & eventually we found our way out of the woods. I've never been in NYC and simply not been able to find another soul. It ended up being a great - and sweaty! - day and its still one of our favorite places. Oh, and I married him in a park too.
My husband proposed to me while we were walking through the park, overlooking the water. :)
we met for scrabble and coffee... I'm no longer sure how many times. 13? once, I played gib with my last 3 tiles for a possible victory, neither of us sure if it was really a word. we flirtingly debated the reality of its existence until someone next to us chimed in, "neutered male ferret"
We were friends back in college in California, but it wasn't until we both ended up in New York the summer post-graduation that we found out about our mutual interest. Funnily enough, we stumbled upon each others' OkCupid profiles and set something up. I'd never been on a date before, nor had he. We got sushi in the West Village, wandered aimlessly, got drinks, and ended up at a comedy show in the East Village. We shared a kiss later that night - my first - and went home. We're still together.
We weren't officially dating, but she helped me wash and dry everything I owned - despite the risk of getting bedbugs herself. We spent hours at the Laundromat, talking and joking, and for that blissful afternoon I forgot that my life had been upturned by a bunch of blood-sucking terrors. Though honestly, I probably owe those guys thanks for bringing us closer.
We had a casual dinner at one of my favorite spots in the South Street Seaport and walked to the pier where we talked for a while, held hands, and it started raining. We kissed and I walked her back to her train where we kissed again. We aren't together but that doesn't stop it from being an amazing memory.
A few years ago, Gabrielle and I went to Lincoln Center for Tango lessons at the midsummer night swing series. During the open dance, it started to rain, then pour. In love, we just kept dancing in the rain. After a while we were soaked and starving. We dashed down the street toward The Park and ducked into the first restaurant we saw, Picholine. In shorts and dripping, we asked the Maitre D' if we were underdressed. He looked us up and down and without hesitation he replied "Of course not".
He had returned to New York after a few grinding years in Silicon Valley and asked me to dinner. I had read the 2-year span of news about what he had made and experienced, but here he was in the flesh, and we both exhaled in relief. We hugged and I realized that I missed him all along; my palms were sweaty like they had been when we kissed in his apartment years before. I picked at an appetizer and gulped wine, unconsciously bracing for what became our love story, our tomorrow.
He asked to kiss me, I said yes. Although the kiss wasn't that great, it was a first kiss for both of us. When I opened my eyes, it was sunset. Summer lightning was dancing above the city skyline, fireworks were literally shooting off over the harbor and for a moment, I felt so happy.
I met a guy online while I was living in Atlanta and he was on the UES. After deciding to take a leap of faith and pursue each other, I flew up to New York for our second date. He took me to Sleep No More.  We kissed in a dark corner but were quickly caught by a disapproving attendant. The whole performance will forever be reflective of my impression of New York - strange, erotic, romantic, aggressive and slightly mental. A few dates later and I was here permanently.
Growing up in Queens, of Colombian descent, I was trying to woo this beautiful, petite, "firecracker" of a girl from Ireland that I worked with. I wanted to impress her with something from her part of the world, so we went to the Lincoln Plaza theater to see... "The Crying Game" !!! 22 years later through thick and thin, married, with 2 great teenagers... I still never know what to expect.
On our second date,  Jake who is now my husband, laughed at me as I screamed on The Cyclone every time the rollercoaster took a dive. He showed me a mischievous side that I didn't see on our first date because we were both nervous. Beneath the sun, his eyes were so light and beautiful. That summer day, I fell little in love with my future husband, even when he relentless bumped into me at the Bump Your Ass off bumper car ride :)
We went to see our favorite musician for my birthday and it was one of the most beautiful concerts I've ever seen. I tried to hide it, but I cried during the last song because I knew that our relationship would end soon.
A former college rower took me on a boat ride in Central Park for our second date. He was very good at rowing. I, on the other hand, was terrible and not all that interested in rowing. It was a lovely date, but unfortunately, it did not work out.
We are from Buffalo and traveled to NYC to try and get pregnant. Came away from our date with now 2.5 year old twin boys!
It was scorching, and my date from N.J. was running about an hour late. I guess that's karma for you. We went to the MET; he was an art major. He admitted to walking from Port Authority on 41st. I politely hinted that he use the restroom as he was sweating from head to toe. He declined, so I made sure not to go near him. I knew more about the exhibits than him. After, he suggested to this native New Yorker we go to Olive Garden aka a tourist trap. Waiting some more, we ate and parted.
A warm and sunny summer evening, I saw him standing at 72nd and Broadway. I could tell it was him by his guardedly expectant stance. My train was late so he thought I might be standing him up. I gave him a hug to say hello and apologize for the 1 train, and we spent the next 5 hours talking as we rambled from the Pier 1 Cafe(excellent view) to the Boat Basin(rowdy crowd) to a restaurant for dinner. His was not my only first date at the Pier 1 Cafe, but it was certainly the best, I married him!
It was probably one of the shortest dates I've been on, but definitely one of the best. I met My date on Prince St. in Soho and we had a nice chat and walked to Hudson River Park. We chose a bench and chatted about our pasts, out ambitions, our bad relationships all while watching one of the most beautiful sunsets in NYC. I think two hours passed before we got up and left. I walked her to the train and kissed her. We don't talk anymore, but I remember that date...and it was beautiful.
It's a date we'd take about once a week,all through summer 2014. On sweltering nights, we would walk the two miles from our new apartment together to an ice cream shop, then to the Williamsburg waterfront to watch the sun go down. Then walk blissfully home, hopefully to a cooler apartment.The ice cream shop is now closed, but we're still going strong.
We danced all night to disco music. My camera actually got stolen from my purse but I didn't even panic because I was having the best time. We've been dating for 5 years and recently moved in together.
I had been out in the rain, came in the restaurant soaking wet. Thank god it wasn't a first date. It was such a cute, nice restaurant. My date was someone who I've known for awhile but we recently reconnected. It wasn't just the place, it was the company.
He told me he's just not that into me, then proceeded to flirt with my friend. At Tout va Bien!
My high-school/college sweetheart and I waited on line for free tickets to the Shakespeare Theater's offering for that evening. Armed with our "passports to Elizabethan England" and a picnic basket, we spread a blanket upon a grassy knoll in the shadow of the Delacorte  Castle weather observatory, where we waited to hear the alert to be seated. We loved each other and, all around us, the people from all walks of life who were also lovers of summertime adventures in New York City … 55 years ago.
She wanted sushi from a five-star restaurant, I wanted hot dogs from a street vendor. She paid for a cab to the tackle shop, I bought the bait, and we went Dutch on the pole. After a trip to the E.R. (I was so nervous, my hands wouldn’t stop shaking when I tried to putting that first worm on the hook) we spent the entire early-September evening fishing in the East River. We didn’t get a single nibble, but boy did I reel in a whopper. Seven years later, I think it’s safe to say she’s a keeper.
I showed up to our first date in Astoria - brunch and the beach. He nonchalantly introduced me to his mom and as we got into the car, I was told we'd all go pick up his dad on the way to the beach. I spent the next two hours on the road with total strangers, waiting anxiously for it all to end. Instead, it was a blast and that was two years ago! He laughs that he never would have gotten my attention without a shock like that. I guess he was right...
My current boyfriend and I spent our first date drunkly and happily wandering around the Met. From there we danced across Central Park to the Plaza while listening to "Rebel Yell." We were out for over 6 hours but it felt like so much shorter.
Dude had his phone out on the table while texting his friend. (Why? This is so avoidable.) Sent his buddy a text saying, "I'll meet you in a bit, she's not that good-looking," while I was telling him a story. Spoiler alert: did not see him again.
After a NY summer together, we ended it here in Union Square.  He was off for a job in San Francisco and I was off for my last year of school.  I left him with a love letter, which he reciprocated 4 months later, reigniting our relationship.  This summer is our second together in NY and marks the end of our long-distance relationship that started 4 months after our Union Square breakup.
We were just grabbing a drink after work, but the place is so romantic, with the low lighting and amazing varieties of wine, I realized how much I wanted to kiss her.  But we weren't on a date.  A week later, we'd be kissing at a North Fork vineyard.
It was summer vacation for this New York City school teacher. I went to a fundraiser for then candidate Obama when I met a guy and we could not stop talking to each other. He invited me to Bryant Park to see The Apartment. A year later, during Close Encounter of the Third Kind (again at Bryant Park) he proposed and I said yes. Five years later, we have a four year old son and are having different sorts of summer fun in NYC!
This is 'our' spot- its where we went when we just started to get to know each other. On numerous nights we would visit the tranquil park and talk for hours, sometimes until 3AM! Passing ships, planes overhead, the stars in the sky, and the beautiful river that is lit by the light from the bridges makes this one special spot!
He was a cute teaching assistant at NYU. Clownishly tall.After some Tinder flirting, he suggested we share a joint and a vegan pizza. By the time we got to the pizzeria, we were very stoned and I distinctly recall saying "it's funny how there's no God."That was our only date.
After months of mostly long-distance AOL dating (this was 2008), we met in Prospect Park. Night fell, and we found ourselves walking through Flatbush looking for a place to sit on dark, quiet residential blocks. What should have been an exciting in-person reunion was stilted and weird. Google maps led us to the only open business--Dunkin Donuts. "So...this isn't working," he began. Five minutes later, it was over, and we still had to find the subway home together before saying goodbye.
We went to the Sunshine Cinema to see Synecdoche, New York when it came out. I didn't know him very well, and the mood of the movie ruined what little good mood there was. That's ok, it wasn't a good fit anyway.
Exchanging kisses with my neighbor who I married 40 years ago.
It was the end of the summer after my first year in college. My first boyfriend and I had spent the summer in our hometowns (Baltimore and Austin, respectively) and had reunited a week before the start of our second year at Columbia. We went to Firefighters Field on Roosevelt Island to read Plato, the first assigned text in our Contemporary Civilization course, and to watch a movie in the park after the sun set. We were young and in love and I still remember it as a perfect New York summer day.
This was a second date. After dinner in Chinatown, we went to Dia Chelsea, where they have installed the Dream House. It's a huge warehouse-sized space with a semi-permanent sound installation. There's wall-to-wall white carpet (so you have to take your shoes off), and pillows scattered around. We let the sound wash over us, threw the pillows around, made forts, and made out. It was a great weird New York date.
I was waiting patiently for an online date to show up. It was supposed to happen at Kaffe 1668.  He texted me that he was running late because of transit   Then he said he was switching to taxi instead. Then after another 10 minutes - which by now he was already 30 min late - he texted and said more or less, "forget it. i'm not coming". I guess he thought he had no chance anymore or the date wasn't worth the effort.
It was our very first date.  Despite a late start (3rd inning) and lost tickets, we met for a Yankees game. It was a perfect summer afternoon.  We chatted over beers & burgers, and I guess he liked me because he asked what were we doing the next day.  Although we were both shy and tentative, I finally got up the nerve to hold his hand as we waited for the D Train at 161st Street.  The Yankees lost, but we won.
We landed here after two years serving in the Peace Corps in Ukraine; we had lived 17 hours apart and kept in touch through frequent letters and phone calls, infrequent visits. He found an apartment on the Lower East Side and I came out from CO sight unseen.  We'd never spent more than a few days together in the same place. That first night we had Famous Ray's Pizza sitting on towels on the floor.  Two kids and 14 years later, he's my best friend and the best thing that ever happened to me.
My friend was working on a movie with a colleague and invited him and me separately to dinner at his house. The colleague came with a date and I came alone. At dinner thecolleague sat with his date on one side and me on the other. We barely exchanged words since he was with a very boisterous  date. Our host who was sitting across from us thought his colleague should be with me and not his date. A few days later he asked each of us if we wanted to go on a date. We've been married for 31 years!
He suggested to check out Figment project and it was our first time to Governors Island. We laid on the grass of a field overlooking lower Manhattan view, played mini golf and a little football, checked out some cool arts and explored the whole island. I thought we had a great time until two days later he told me he doesn't think we are a match. Nevertheless, it was a great date.
During the week I turned 21, my aunt went to Europe and let me stay in her little Greenwich Village apartment. The eve and night before my birthday, I stayed up most of the night with the guy I had been dating, and we, amicably, broke up. The next morning, the guy I really liked came over and took me out for breakfast. Ah, 21 ...
It was Restaurant Week 2013 at Club A Steakhouse, and were thrilled to have Malbec and buttery calamari after a long day of moving my now fiancé into his new apartment. Ten minutes in, the ceiling AC unit gurgled and poured a pint of black sludgy water into our wine, entrees, and laps. The horrified waiter apologized profusely, then reappeared with a new bottle (and a half) of wine and double portions of our appetizers. We were so drunk, full, and giggly – it's one of our favorite dates.
This was a 2nd date where the date proceeded to tell me about his last relationship and how childish his ex was.  He said the police were involved. I proceeded to say something like, "How old are we?!"  That's when he decided to drink/dine and dash. He just got up and left. I tried to cancel the chicken he had ordered but it was too late. I told the staff that they could have it since I didn't eat meat. They felt bad and didn't charge me for his meal. I stayed to eat my meal and finish my drink.
We finally found the perfect spot. We started out walking around soho, stopped by the nyu campus, and grabbed brunch and tea and his favorite shop. We wanted to sit in the grass and just relax in the sun, but didn't want to make the trek to the busy, tourist filled Central Park. He remembered a fun spot near Juilliard that was less known. When we got there, I don't think he realized just how much I fell in love. In love with the city, in love with nature, and more importantly, in love with him.
We met at a mutual acquaintance's gathering five years ago and had a brief fling followed by an awkward friendship.  Five years later we got together to catch up near the entrance to Prospect Park at Grand Army Plaza and haven't said goodbye yet.
It was his first time in the city, and I was trying to convince him to move here. He seemed jittery and uncomfortable all day, and I decided he would never want to live in the city. Turns out, he was nervous because he was planning to propose and had the ring in his pocket. He popped the question and a photo was taken that went on a billboard in the middle of Time's Square. We moved here less than a year later.
It was about a 6 months into dating my boyfriend.  He wanted to take me to "his" part of Brooklyn.  He took my to lunch in one of the little hole in the wall restaurants on the canal.  It was a a beautiful day so we decided to go for a long walk.  We walked through Manhattan Beach, Brighton and Coney Island along the boardwalk.  It was a simple date but we were so in love and enjoyed each others company that it didn't matter what we did; we just wanted to be together.
We were both still reeling from difficult divorces.  Searching online for friendship, I was taken by a look in her eye.  We met and quickly discovered we were at same college in the 70s, shared some close friends but had never heard of the other!  Having been so vetted, we have been together ever since...five years and, oh, who's counting?!
I had just moved into my first NYC apartment and was on a budget. My boyfriend and I were going to Jersey City to watch fireworks from the Goldman Sachs building with a friend of his later, so we sat in Battery Park first. On the way to the PATH we found a perfect mirror on the street. My boyfriend carried it all the way to New Jersey, and then back to the Upper East Side, for me to hang in my new room.
In 1992, NYC held a Desert Storm fireworks display over the water in lower Manhattan.  I met my date (now wife) and we walked down to the promenade to see the show.  We stood together in silence, watching the fireworks light up the sky, reflecting off the buildings along the FDR drive.  It was magical and I knew then that I could spend the rest of my life with her.  I asked her to marry me later that year.
We met on a first  date  (courtesy of OkCupid) for a Mumford concert at the Forest Hills Tennis Stadium in Queens. It was a win win for me since he was so cute and they were my favorite band. As we were entering the concert he kissed me. We have recreated that moment recently (almost 2 years later!) at The Who concert at the same theater. The beat goes on!
I was at a Balkan music concert because my friend knew the accordionist. A guy approached me and asked for my number (he ended up being the roommate of the band's drummer). We met up later that week (he asked me out for coffee or hot chocolate or beer...we ended up getting a beer) and more than a year and a half later we are are still together. I even learned Hebrew for him since he's from Israel!
Walked in, grabbed a number, walked out with cannolis, took them to Washington Square Park.  We sat under the arch until it got chilly and, content to stay together longer, took a cab home to watch "Love Actually". It was the first time I kissed someone in a taxi.
He hired 2 actors to read a script about our how we met and our first years together. Without telling me! They were next to us and I couldn't understand how they got this story. I turned back to my partner and he was down on one knee.
We had been friendly in college but reconnected our first year out of school when we were both living in New York. This small garden just north of Washington Square Park was a quick stop during the most effortless first date I've ever had. Today, we are still finding new places to enjoy summer dates in our city.
we met a week before he graduated, a week before he began to prepare for the bar exam.  So instead of a summer spent exploring the city, we met for the hour long break he took every evening. We walked in Riverside Park. One memory is a picnic at Grant's Tomb. I had laid out everything when the guard came striding to us and told us we were on federal property.  Then he took pity and said that if we moved down one step, we'd be fine.  the two bottom steps were state property and not his business.
One of those meet-your-soulmate-on-the-subway moments turned wrong. I had headphones in and was riding the D train from organic chemistry class to work. He was cute so I took out my headphones and he asked me on a date before getting off the train. Even though I had a significant other, I said yes because I was intrigued. He turned out to be the strangest guy and was basically a deadbeat....and smoked cigarettes the whole date – ew!
Beautiful girl came and got coffee from me every morning for a year or so. We're both painfully shy, but on my last day working at the cafe, I got the courage to ask her out. We've been together just over two years now.
A fellow I'd known for 20 years in church circles (and who was getting divorced after 25) announced on Facebook that he'd won two tickets to 'The Bacchae' in the Shakespeare in the Park virtual lottery. Did anyone want his other ticket? 'Me! Me! Me!' I posted on his wall. We met for a picnic supper. It was awkward. We didn't know if we were on a date or what. Eventually, we figured it out. We've been living together now for 5 years. Two gray-haired Quakers owe it all to Euripides and Joe Papp.
After enjoying the many great views from Roosevelt Island we retreated to a quiet corner in the greenery of the park at the island's southern tip; too quiet, apparently, as park security missed us on the last lap and locked the very tall fence with us inside, unable to get over with our bikes. Luckily they only changed one number on the combination, and we lingered a bit longer in our private park once we knew we could leave.
I agreed to coffee with an OK Cupid date. For some reason, he said we should meet at the Toys 'R' Us in Times Square. After confirming the date via e-mail twice, he showed up 20 minutes late and then immediately suggested we head to Korea Town to grab lunch there. I thought we should just stay in area. We waded our way through throngs of tourists to get to an over-priced diner where I had a $12 bowl of chicken noodle soup.
Knowing that Dumbo is my favorite place he asked me to show him around there because he had never been.  We walked across the Brooklyn Bridge.  I took him to a cool Thai restaurant. We walked along the water. Got ice cream from the ice cream factory and sat on the grass while watching the sunset behind the Brooklyn Bridge.  We have been together for 6 years :)
We have been dating for about a month. At the most beautiful and sweetest moment, when we sat in a chapel enjoying choir, he said to me he liked small and beautiful church just like me... However, within 24 hour, he told me that he wanted to break up, and the idea came out when we were at chapel... I was totally shocked. It is so out of nowhere and all of sudden.
My boyfriend and I had been in a long distance between New York and Tel Aviv for eight months. While he was visiting, we planned to get married at City Hall and then celebrate at Gramercy Tavern. I backed out the ceremony the day before, but we went to the dinner anyway. My boyfriend (who, three years later, is now my husband) was understanding and empathetic toward my reservations about a City Hall wedding and he made that night at Gramercy Tavern unforgettable. The food wasn't bad, either..
I was looking forward to a fourth date of bowling after holding out hope for some spark. We had to wait for a lane so we played mini golf to kill the time. He was clearly angry that I won, and once we started bowling, celebrated when he did better than me. We barely interacted during 6 games, then I offered to pay because he had paid every other date. It turned out that it was per player per game so the "fun" costed 150 dollars. He ended up paying back part of it, but it was over.
Went to dinner at a pretty good / trendy tapas-style restaurant. Afterwards, we wanted to hang out in Madison Square Park. She wanted dessert. There was McDonalds. Bam. 5 Minutes later she's walking out in her 4 inch heals with a full value meal and McFlurry. Can you say marry me? Someday...
It was cloudy during the very last week where summer is hanging on before turning to fall. We sat on a bench, drinking coffee I had brought from the cafe across the street. We had survived long distance, the move to New York, difficult families, different religions, unemployment, depression, and 13 speeding tickets. After 6 years of magic and dates and fights and firsts, I cried as we ended our relationship. Then we went out for burgers.
We were headed to Massachusetts by train to be with my family that weekend. He was visiting me from Spain for three weeks as he does every August. I was meeting him after work and when I finally found him in the maze that is Penn Station, I dropped my bag and ran to him. An older woman nearby started smiling at us. Everyone else passed by with glazed-over Penn Station gloom.
Looba booba was her nick name. Our first date we went to a bar where she pulled out her wallet. I noticed a picture and said, "Nice! Are that your niece?" She looked at me, concerned and was silent. "No, that's my daughter." I told her it was sexy and we spent the next few hours watching a meteor shower on my roof in Bed Stuy. Didn't catch meteors, but we enjoyed a chilled, sparkling Rose, perfect for the hot July night. She spent the night, and I haven't seen her since.
My boyfriend Tom took me for a walk into strawberry fields. As a john Lennon fan who moved to nyc 18 months before, I often used to go and sit there. This time was different. After a little while sitting on the bench dedicated to 'thom hunter', he produced a ring and asked me to marry him. That was 13 years ago on July 1st. The perfect summer nyc date!
After a few email exchanges with someone I met online, we agreed to meet.  Unsure of where to go/what to do, we agreed that I would bring a blanket and food, and he would bring wine and we could relax and talk.  We met at 4, laid out the blanket, ate, talked, laughed and watched the sun go down.  By 11pm, we were the only two on the grass under the stars.  A very sweet first date.
It wasnt until our 2nd drink that I found out she was just as nervous about our 1st date. We had once met over a yr ago when a college friend was in town for a wkend to visit his sister, my date. Just last wk I ran into her again, of all places, on a dating site. I was nervous when I reached out to her, and excited when she responded. A few sips into our 2nd drink she looked up at and me and said, “I didn’t know what to expect tonight. But I’m pleasantly surprised." "Me too." And she said,
Matt & Kim were highlighting Village Voice's Siren Fest 2010 (RIP Siren Fest :-(). The date was like our romance: warm, fun, filled with beaches and junk food, and over all too soon. Matt & Kim started their set as we rode the rollercoaster. It'll always be one of my fondest memories, the rollercoaster hurtling down toward Coney Island, and us throwing our hands up as this great carney tunes of this ridiculously fun duo from Brooklyn rocked out and celebrated life.
Went out with a woman I'd known through a friend & online for a year, had a great dinner at Dojo's, then caught some bands at Terra Blues.  Couple came in with a pizza box, opened it onto a candle, it caught fire spectacularly, and I leaped up and put it out with my hands.  The woman was very impressed and we're a couple now, things are going well; no more fires thankfully.
i was fourteen years old, on a date with a private school boy whose sweet talk was all about his political aspirations and how he meant to achieve them. At about 11 o'clock , we found ourselves alone stairs of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. A Volkswagen Beetle suddenly pulled up to the curb, the doors let out a blasting waltz and a couple in black tie who danced until the music ended, bowed, and silently sped off into the night. I thought " that's what romance is" and never saw the boy again.
After ordering dinner, my date stepped outside and proceeded to take a 45 minute phone call (not hyperbole) without even a check-in. I looked around the block for him once after about 30 minutes. No go. I figured he left. I eventually paid and was about to leave when he knocked on the window, stormed in and yelled and berated me for "not trusting him enough" to come back after his call. The call wasn't an emergency. Just a chat. Worst. Date. Ever.
We had a picnic on the lawn at Snug Harbor, and enjoyed the peace and tranquility of the Chinese Scholars Garden. It was special to discover a new place I had never been, with this new person in my life. I only realized years later that she grew up a couple of blocks from there, and that her parents still lived there at the time.  In 2012, after New York State legalized equal marriage, we had a beautiful wedding in a park a short walk from our current home in Brooklyn.
We had met that summer. He went off to college and I went into my senior year of high school. We stayed in touch and saw each other every month when he visited. While we didn't know what we officially "were" for a long time, our first real date was to the old Whitney museum (he was a Fine Arts major) and then to Buttercup Bake Shop (now closed on the UWS). He was my first love and we dated for 4 years after that.
It was our first date. I thought we'd keep it simple, short, and noncommittal. A quick walk through union square on the hottest day of July with 90% humidity drinking Spanish iced lattes. I gave him the history of the metronome art installation. He gave me a pack of sunflower seeds (my favorite flowers) and we planted it in the garden using a spork. We are married now and visit often. The sunflowers never grew, but our love continues to 3 years later.
Going home together, staying up all night talking, waking up next to you, eating breakfast sandwiches, being tired but so happy, holding your hand in an empty zoo, seeing tigers and reptiles, putting my hands in your pocket, leaning on your shoulder on the subway, spending 24 hours & laughing at your friend who was scared of raisins were some of the things we did for the first time together that day. It was also the first time I knew I wanted to spend every other day with you.
We are both over 50 and came out of unhappy marriages that had been happy at the beginning. What's different this time is not that we became flawless together. What's different is that when we see the potential potholes, we are able to talk about it. And for the rest of the time, we enjoy it. We dance tango, we take walks in the city, we go to the beach, I even learned to ski. And we laugh a lot. That too.
During the last week of summer, we exchanged quick pleasantries online, met for a rooftop drink at the Peninsula, and knew we clicked. Kindness and sincerety go a long way. The next 9 months together were a whirlwind!
We biked around Red Hook, had Steve's Key Lime Pie, had a drink at Bait and Tackle, then went back to his nearby apartment and grilled on the roof. And then there were actual fireworks over lower Manhattan, which we both found amusing. Led to a good summer romance. The relationship didn't last but it was a top notch summer/first date.
It took him 23 hours to get to NY because he couldn't afford a direct flight. Once he got here I became extremely sick. He took care of me for a week. The first place and last place I took him to was The Top of the Rock. He left the next day but today I'm with him.
I've been on quite a few dates before and not once have I had a good date with someone who goes to school at Columbia University. However this date took takes the gold in bad dates. He comes in an hour late, never apologizes, and continues to brag about how his life is so cultured. As he continues to talk about his oh-so sophisticated life, I can't help but stare at the food stuck in his teeth.  He doesn't pick up the check and I end up paying for his $20 appetizer. I'll stick with NYU guys.
We walked around in the freezing cold and needed to find a place to warm up. Stumbled upon this great Ethiopian place as they were serving some Ethiopian coffee and delicious food.
June 28th, a birthday, a second date, we met at the subway and rode it to the botanical gardens. my eyes were watering from allergies and at the same time that I asked for a tissue you pulled out a present for me that you had wrapped IN a tissue.
After meeting a guy at a wine tasting event one hot July evening, he asked me out on a date. He chose The Frying Pan, for it's cool breeze and hot location. We met on a Sunday afternoon for lunch, and after looking over the menu, I exclaimed, "They have lobster!" I protested, and said, I will have something else. My date insisted that I get it and ordered it immediately. The date went well but the relationship didn't last. To this day, my friends fondly remember him as "Lobster Lunch".
We planned to meet on Labor Day at the Brooklyn Museum but forgot it was the Caribbean Day Parade on Eastern Parkway! This was before cell phones; I figured we would never find each other in the huge crowd and was about to give up when somehow I just bumped into him.  Then we escaped the crowds into Prospect Park and got caught in a sudden summer thunderstorm. It was a totally romantic afternoon but I was young and shy and didn't know how to make anything happen. We only had that one date.
My boyfriend and I went rowing at the lake by the Loeb Boathouse in Central Park. Just a heads up, it is cash only but it's relatively inexpensive. It was such a treat to be  surrounded by the tranquil park with ducks and other rowers. It's like stepping into a painting. We followed rowing with wine and then dinner overlooking the water at the romantic Loeb Boathouse Restaurant. It was a memorable and sweet summer date.
On our first date, I asked him to enter the park from 85th St and to find me at one of the benches near the third lamp post wearing a mustard trench coat. Then after a few dates, I invited him to my apartment, which was bare, had no pictures of family or friends, and looked like I could pack up in 10 minutes and leave. The mailbox downstairs didn't even have my name of it. He thought I was a spy!!!  And the name stuck. We've been together ever since!
15 years ago, after a beautiful afternoon sitting on the warm grass in a Central Park field, a wonderful woman agreed to join me for supper at Tavern on the Green.  Several hours later, a passion ignited that burns to this day.  Each morning I get to say ... GMILY - Good Morning I Love You.
About 5 years ago, to the day actually, my wife and I met and very quickly began to do "Key to the City" together.  For our first outing we went to Queens.  We started with lunch at Ben's Deli (not part of the route) and then visited Tortilleria Nixtamal, the Louis Armstrong House Museum, the Office of New York City Council Member Daniel Dromm and Eddie's Sweet Shop.  It was a perfect Day.
I had just returned from 4 years away from home, attending college.  In those days, no social media, so, a blind date was arranged with an "up & coming young doctor."  He came to pick me up at my parents' home (where I was living temporarily).  He was head to toe, dressed in polyester &  I was dressed to go clubbing.  After a movie... I suggested going for drinks.  He suggested going for ice cream.  I felt like I should have been at a "sock hop" & wearing a sweater twin set.  Done & done.
We met at a cute cafe in TriBeCa at 6:15. He said he should be able to be there. I was green enough to wait 1 hour before I was walking out the door. Made him take me out to dinner where I listened to him talk about himself all night and smell his awful coffee breath. Next time, 15 mins tops.
I'm not dating the guy anymore, but it was probably my favorite date in NYC in the last 2 years. The boat takes you up and down the east river at dusk. It's rustic and cutely appointed. The food was decent. There's an upper deck where you can have drinks before/during/after dinner. And best of all it's not touristy like other dinner cruises.
For our 5th date, we decided roller coasters and hot dogs were a great idea. My desire to impress him trumped my intense fear of heights and we took on the Thunderbolt as the first ride. The adrenaline provided an underlining excitement in both us with a sense of adventure. We took on the park, hit the candy store for bags full of old school sugar treats and stopped at Rita's for ice cream. Perfect date!
Eight summers ago, my now-wife & I were in the awkward phase of a relationship where you're "friends," but hanging out all the time and hoping something more happens. Both young and new to NYC, no corner of the city seemed like too long of a train ride or too out of the way to want to explore, especially on a warm summer night, and we decided to walk around Roosevelt Island. It was sitting by the lighthouse that we finally summed up the courage to tell each other how we REALLY felt.
I met a handsome man in a gay bar, back in the '70s, we hit it off real well. After a night of no sleep at his place, he said, "I've tickets to Pippin this week; want to go?""Sure, I said, tell me when, and I'll show up."I did; he was there, beaming. Ben Vereen was amazing. Intermission came, he said, "I've got to use the bathroom."He left and never returned.
I was fifteen and he was sixteen. We ran hand in hand up the stairs to the rooftop of the Manhattan School of Music building between classes on a sunny Saturday.  The air was warm, leaves were bright green and, our hearts pounding with excitement, we shared a kiss.  As if on cue, the bells of neighboring Riverside Church began ringing - it happened to be noon but it was dramatically romantic - and we broke into laughter.  We didn't end up a couple after all, but it is a beautiful memory.
We met at 1 Bowling Green, and he told me that when he moved to NY, he did walking historical tours of Manhattan and they started at that location. He explained how his exploration of the city ultimately led him to his career choice. Not only was it romantic to walk around holding hands & listening to him recite the fascinating history, but hearing his personal story about something he was passionate about made me swoon. We didn’t ultimately work out, but it was still the best date of my life.
At an evening party on a balcony in Carroll Gardens.  He asked me to stand on the chair with him so he could show me the Statue of Liberty all lit up.  What a beautiful sight!  And there we had a long and passionate first kiss.

Q.
Why do many health insurers pay for the shingles vaccine only for people who are 60 or older?
A.
The reasoning has to do with the special nature of the shingles infection and with how the immune system changes as people age.
Shingles is a reactivation of varicella zoster, the virus that causes chickenpox.
Aging people produce fewer and fewer of the immune cells that are recruited and trained to fight new infections, so-called naïve T-cells, and so they are less reactive to most vaccines,
the National Institute on Aging explains
.
But those who have had chickenpox still have a supply of the “memory” T-cells they produced to fight the original infection. The vaccine for shingles relies on these cells, making it particularly effective in older people.
The vaccine has been approved for those as young as 50,
the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says
, but there is no recommendation for routine use by those under 60, because there are no long-term studies showing how long the shot remains effective in people ages 50 to 59.
There is
solid evidence
showing that it remains effective for up to five years in the older age bracket.
“Protection beyond five years is uncertain,” the C.D.C. says in its fact sheet on the vaccine. “Therefore, adults receiving the vaccine before age 60 years might not be protected when their risks for shingles and its complications are greatest.”

It’s the sort of game people play to be reassured of each other’s devotion. After the morning Danya and Addison have had — beginning with a bout of bad sex and getting worse from there — they probably need the affirmation.
“Would you still love me if I was 300 pounds, had a mustache and only took a shower once a week?”
“I’d still love you, but I would miss you a lot.”
“Would you still love me if I was in a horrible fire and was not recognizable?”
“As long as you and I were breathing the same air.”
In “Would You Still Love Me If … ,” an ungainly
new play by John S. Anastasi,
erratically directed by
Kathleen Turner
at New World Stages, the more pertinent question on Danya’s mind is whether Addison (Rebecca Brooksher) would still love her if she were a man.
Two years into their relationship, 28-year-old Danya (Sofia Jean Gomez) isn’t courageous enough to confess to her partner that she has always felt male — though she manages to break it to her formidable mother, Victoria (Ms. Turner), and is already in talks with a surgeon (Roya Shanks) to align her body with her gender identity.
It’s a topical setup, yet this diligently educational play has the feel of a bad television movie, its ginned-up plot rife with implausibilities. Addison secretly found a baby to adopt months ago, she and Danya have to sign the papers this very afternoon, and the birth mother insists the child not go to a man? Really?
That Ms. Turner keeps the production from teetering into camp is an achievement in itself, but that danger may be what makes the show so nervous about humor. It never finds its tone.
Yet Ms. Turner, who last month
replaced the original director,
Nona Gerard, has no trouble melding comedy and pain in her own very smart performance.
“This is all my fault. I am so sorry,” Victoria says in that whiskey-and-cigarettes voice when Danya first tells her the news. “They sprayed the whole house with pesticides in my second trimester.”
The yearning at the heart of this play — that love will be strong enough to survive bodily transformation — is the same longing that drives Craig Lucas’s
“Prelude to a Kiss,”
one of the catalog of AIDS plays from the late 1980s and early ’90s, when another stigmatized subculture was emerging into popular consciousness.
Mr. Anastasi is relatively early in responding to this historical moment. More plays about transgender experience will follow, and with them, perhaps, more poetry.

WASHINGTON —  Five months before a United Nations summit meeting aimed at forging a historic global accord to cut climate-warming emissions, significant signs of progress toward an agreement are emerging.
China
, the world’s largest greenhouse gas polluter, submitted a 16-page plan to the United Nations on Tuesday detailing how it plans to shift its economy to reduce fossil fuel emissions by 2030. On the same day, President
Dilma Rousseff
of
Brazil
, which is among the top 10 carbon emitters, and
President Obama
announced in Washington
that their nations had agreed to sharply expand electricity generation from renewable sources.
But it is increasingly evident that the policy actions by these countries and others will not be enough to stave off a rise in the atmospheric temperature of 2 degrees Celsius, or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit. At that point, scientists say, the planet will be locked into a future of extreme storms, droughts, food and water shortages, and rising sea levels.
Under
a United Nations accord reached in Peru
last December, every nation is to submit a plan for cutting carbon emissions well ahead of the December summit meeting in Paris. The plans by the individual nations will form the core of the new agreement.
South Korea, Serbia and Iceland also submitted their plans for cutting emissions on Tuesday, joining the 40 or so countries that had already done so, including Canada, Mexico, Russia and the United States, along with the European Union.
And in the joint announcement by Brazil and the United States, the two nations committed to increasing the use of wind, solar and
geothermal
energy to make up 20 percent of each country’s electricity production by 2030, which would double power generation from renewable sources in Brazil and triple it in the United States. Brazil also pledged to restore about 30 million acres of Amazon rain forest, an area about the size of Pennsylvania.
“Following progress during my trips to China and India, this shows that the world’s major economies can begin to transcend some of the old divides and work together to confront the common challenge that we face — something that we have to work on for future generations,” said Mr. Obama, who has pushed other countries to sign on to a
climate change
deal.
Christiana Figueres, the top United Nations climate change official, said, “Over the past 24 hours, we’ve seen a very nice example of the diversity of countries engaging on the climate solution.” But she added, “The sum total of these does not get us to 2 degrees.”
Climate policy experts pointed to the significance of China’s plan in particular. The United States and China, the world’s top greenhouse gas polluters, have long been viewed as the biggest obstacles to reaching a meaningful global warming deal. That changed last November when
Mr. Obama and President Xi Jinping jointly announced
that the United States would lower its emissions up to 28 percent from 2005 levels by 2025, while China’s emissions would peak and then decline no later than 2030.

In March, Mr. Obama submitted a plan to the United Nations detailing how the United States would meet its target. It said it would do so chiefly through enactment of Environmental Protection Agency regulations on emissions from cars, trucks and power plants.
China’s plan included a broad commitment to decouple economic growth from the use of fossil fuels, and a move to lower its carbon intensity, or the amount of the pollutant generated by each point of economic growth, by 60 to 65 percent from 2005 levels by 2030. It also laid out plans to develop a national
cap-and-trade
system, a market-based program for reducing emissions in which companies must pay for permits to pollute, and can buy and sell those permits among themselves.
“It demonstrates the depth of climate policy architecture,” said David Sandalow, a fellow at the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University and a former top Energy Department official in the Obama administration. “It’s very detailed and suggests the seriousness with which China takes its climate policy goals.”
In his first term, Mr. Obama tried unsuccessfully to push a similar cap-and-trade system through Congress.
“There is a lot of irony that the U.S., which invented free-market approaches to stopping climate change, is using command-and-control regulations while Communist China will use a carbon market,” said Paul Bledsoe, a top climate change official in the administration of former President Bill Clinton.
But Brazil, despite its announcement on Tuesday, has not yet submitted its climate plan to the United Nations, and several other major polluting economies, including India and Japan, also have not. In any event, climate policy experts say it is almost certain that their plans will not add up to strong enough action to curb the harmful effects of climate change.
Ms. Figueres and other United Nations negotiators say they now see a Paris accord as a first step in a multiyear process in which countries will put forth domestic climate policies and reconvene regularly to make their plans more stringent.
“It’s not a one-shot deal,” she said. “It’s like a highway, with each country going in the lane with the speed that they can go. Some will start out slowly and speed up later. It will be a progressive process over time.”
One hurdle to a pact is Republican lawmakers’ longstanding opposition to participation in a global climate change deal. They say that such a plan could hurt the American economy, while allowing other countries to continue to pollute at higher levels. Senator James M. Inhofe, Republican of Oklahoma, who is the chairman of the Senate Environment Committee, said he was deeply skeptical of China’s plan.
“China’s commitment to reduce carbon emissions is unattainable and unrealistic,” Mr. Inhofe said in a statement. “China’s commitment will allow the country to continue increasing its emissions for the next 15 years.”
Money is another major obstacle. In 2009, Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton pledged that by 2020, developed economies would send $100 billion annually, from both public and private sources, to developing economies to help them adapt to the ravages of climate change. This year, the United Nations has sought to establish a $10 billion “Green Climate Fund” to help begin that fund-raising effort.
Although Mr. Obama has pledged $3 billion — more than any other nation has offered — Republicans in Congress have blocked efforts to appropriate the money.
Climate policy experts say that without the money from rich countries, developing economies will not be able to follow through on their pledges.

If you don’t mind the church full of parishioners who are slaughtered to the sounds of Lynyrd Skynyrd’s “
Free Bird
” or the “Arab terrorists” who are blown to smithereens or the guns that are pointed at pet dogs or the human heads that explode like firebombed melons as “Pomp and Circumstance” plays, it may be possible to enjoy “Kingsman: The Secret Service.” That said, as this bludgeoning movie grinds to a halt, its gears clogged by viscera and narrative overkill, even those who enjoy go-go gore may end up yearning for the soft touch and subtleties of Guy Ritchie.
The British director Matthew Vaughn first came to attention as a producer on “
Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels
,” Mr. Ritchie’s jokey, blunt-force gangster caper. Mr. Vaughn then went on to direct a Ritchie-esque gangster flick of his own, “
Layer Cake
,” now best remembered for Daniel Craig’s star-making turn. Since then, Mr. Vaughn has directed the ultraviolent “
Kick-Ass
” movies and a franchise reboot (“
X-Men: First Class
”), both of which have raked in enough cash to assure that he’ll be running amok for a while. He’s developed into an adequate if often generic manager of action and bodies, but his real talent is for delivering extreme violence with a shrug and a smile.
The problem is that Mr. Vaughn has no interest in, or perhaps understanding of, violence as a cinematic tool. He doesn’t use violence; he squanders it. Some directors overdo it with crane shots, close-ups and dissolves, but Mr. Vaughn gorges on splatter, splashing rooms with red until it’s the only color and emotional note left. His love for guns and guts at least made sense in the “Kick-Ass” movies, mondo fairy tales about a child killer who locks and loads on the run. But his lack of modulation ruins “Kingsman,” which is based on a comic book by Mark Millar and Dave Gibbons, and was written by Mr. Vaughn
with his frequent collaborator Jane Goldman
.
That’s too bad, because someone here has assembled a fine cast led by
Colin Firth
, who plays a spy in an agency hidden behind (and beneath) a
Savile Row
tailor shop where he swaps tradecraft secrets with Michael Caine,
Mark Strong
and the charming newcomer Taron Egerton. A lisping Samuel L. Jackson plays the villain, an American zillionaire with a henchwoman (Sofia Boutella) who, like Oscar Pistorius, uses leg prosthetics, though ones that are sharp enough to slice a man in half as cleanly as if he were an overcooked Easter ham. Nothing excites Mr. Vaughn as a director more than turning this chick loose, especially in slow motion with a gun in her pretty hand.
“Kingsman: The Secret Service” is rated R (Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian). Splat.

Live from New York… It’s Hillary Clinton!
Hillary Rodham Clinton is scheduled to appear on “Saturday Night Live” this weekend, the latest — and highest stakes — appearance of her current push to show her funny, personable side as the campaign heads into the critical first Democratic debate and she faces headwinds in Iowa and New Hampshire and a potential challenge from Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.
In a top-secret appearance that her campaign would not confirm, Mrs. Clinton will meet her comedic counterpart, Kate McKinnon, who has portrayed the former first lady to effusive praise as the latest “S.N.L.” member to don a blonde wig and attempt to bring to life the character of Mrs. Clinton.
In order to appear, Mrs. Clinton turned down the chance to give the keynote address to the influential Human Rights Campaign, the country’s most powerful lesbian and gay rights group, which will allow her to make the debut “S.N.L.” appearance of her 2016 campaign, said several people with knowledge of her schedule who could not discuss private planning for attribution.
She is expected to pop in to join Ms. McKinnon as part of the so-called cold open skit, these people said. A spokeswoman for NBC declined to comment.
Both the show and NBC were hoping to make the appearance a splashy surprise. The show’s creator, Lorne Michaels, is well known for being tight-lipped about guests and has even changed the lineup at the last minute, which is still a possibility with Mrs. Clinton, whose own schedule is also fluid, these people said.
In the proposed skit, Mrs. Clinton would likely poke fun at herself for trying to appear more authentic while carefully plotting her path to the presidency. Ms. McKinnon, an unabashed Clinton supporter, told The Times’s Maureen Dowd that Mrs. Clinton was “a staunch, passionate lady, and in our culture, unfortunately, there’s something funny about that.”
In the opening skit on the night before Mrs. Clinton’s announcement in April, Ms. McKinnon, as Mrs. Clinton, prepared for her 2016 run with the help of her red-headed assistant, Kristina (based on the Clinton campaign’s deputy communications director, Kristina Schake).
“Meet my hand in the air!” Ms. McKinnon says, poking fun at the woodenness of Mrs. Clinton’s high-five.
“S.N.L.” has had a long history of depicting Mrs. Clinton. During the Clinton administration, the comedian Jan Hooks was Mrs. Clinton to Phil Hartman’s Bill Clinton. (Ms. Hooks’s Hillary got into a fistfight with Senator Bob Dole.) During Mrs. Clinton’s run for the Senate in New York, Ana Gasteyer portrayed her as a politician desperately trying to appear domestic. (“I can’t wait to prepare some food dishes in this kitchen, such as salads and toast,” Ms. Gasteyer’s Hillary says from her kitchen in Chappaqua, N.Y.)
But the truly memorable impression came during the 2008 presidential campaign when the pants-suit-wearing Amy Poehler portrayed Mrs. Clinton, eventually teaming up with Tina Fey’s Sarah Palin, to comedic gold and a ratings sensation for the long-running late-night show.
In one skit about sexism in the 2008 race, Ms. Fey’s Palin says “Please, stop photo-shopping my head on sexy bikini pictures!” Ms. Poehler’s Hillary adds, “And stop saying I have cankles!”
(Mrs. Clinton, at one point, sneaked off the campaign trail in 2008 to make a surprise appearance alongside Ms. Poehler in a skit that mocked news media bias to Senator Barack Obama and Mrs. Clinton’s guffaw of a laugh.)
In an odd instance of reality imitating art, Mrs. Clinton alluded to an “S.N.L.” skit during a Democratic debate in Ohio in 2008. “In the last several debates, I seem to get the first question all the time,” she told the moderators, who in the “S.N.L.” skit were accused of favoring Mr. Obama. “I don’t mind. I’ll be happy to field it,” Mrs. Clinton said. “I do find it curious and if anybody saw ‘Saturday Night Live,’ maybe we should ask Barack if he’s comfortable and needs another pillow.”
